title: A cold giant planet challenges the usual growth route
freshness: Accepted and in press at The Astrophysical Journal Letters; arXiv version submitted November 11, 2026; preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: Sixteen years of observations have revealed HIP 88962 b, a planet nearly five times Jupiter's mass on a wide, elongated orbit around a low-mass star. Its position and mass are difficult to reproduce with standard planet-growth simulations, raising the possibility that it formed when part of its birth disk collapsed directly.
whyItMatters: Gas giants are often described as solid cores that slowly gathered thick envelopes. HIP 88962 b tests where that explanation stops working and whether some giant planets instead form through the rapid collapse of unstable gas disks.

exploreFurther.label: Boss et al., accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters

whatToExploreNext: What observations can distinguish a giant planet formed by core accretion from one formed by disk instability?

body:
## A slow wobble reveals a distant giant

A cold gas giant nearly five times Jupiter's mass has been found circling a star much lighter than the Sun. HIP 88962 b takes about 19.3 years to complete one orbit and travels on a highly elongated path. At its characteristic orbital distance of 6.15 astronomical units, it sits a little farther from its star than Jupiter does from the Sun.

The host, HIP 88962, is a cool K7 dwarf about 89 light-years away. Its estimated mass is 62 percent of the Sun's. Massive planets are uncommon around such low-mass stars, particularly on wide orbits, which makes this system useful for testing how gas giants form.

Researchers followed the star with the Planet Finder Spectrograph on the Magellan Clay telescope from 2010 to 2025. Across 47 observing epochs on 41 nights, the star's spectral lines shifted back and forth. This radial-velocity signal shows the star moving toward and away from Earth under the planet's gravitational pull. The measured velocity swing has a semiamplitude of 94.9 metres per second.

Radial velocity alone gives only a minimum planet mass because the orbit's tilt is unknown. The team combined that signal with astrometry from Hipparcos and Gaia, which tracks the star's movement across the sky. Their joint fit places the orbit nearly edge-on, with an inclination of 91 plus or minus 22 degrees. It gives the planet a true mass of 4.83 Jupiter masses, a semimajor axis of 6.15 plus or minus 0.5 astronomical units, and an eccentricity of about 0.72. An eccentricity near zero would describe a circle; this much larger value means the star-planet distance changes strongly during each orbit.

## Two ways to build a giant planet

The common core-accretion model starts with dust and rock assembling a solid core. Once that core becomes massive enough, it rapidly captures gas from the surrounding disk. This process works well for many known giant planets, but published population simulations for low-mass stars do not produce planets as massive and distant as HIP 88962 b.

The authors argue that gas-disk gravitational instability is a better match. In that route, a cold, massive region of the young star's disk becomes unstable and collapses under its own gravity, forming a giant object much faster than core accretion would.

That origin was not observed directly. The measured result is the planet's present orbit and mass. Its proposed birth by disk instability comes from comparing those measurements with existing formation models. Other processes, including migration or interactions with additional bodies, could have altered the orbit after formation.

## One planet is secure, a second is not

After subtracting the long-period orbit, the data contain a possible 4.11-day signal. The researchers do not classify it as another planet. Adding a second orbit improves the residual scatter only slightly, while enhanced calcium emission and photometric variability show that the star is active. Rotating starspots and magnetic regions can imitate short-period planetary signals.

The long orbit is also not yet covered perfectly. Alternative fits allow a still longer period, so continued measurements should refine the path. HIP 88962 b is secure enough to challenge formation calculations, but its unusual origin remains a hypothesis for future observations to test.
